warmup.q: A nightly job unpacks 1,000 compressed files and ends with exit code 0, the number a program returns to say "all went well". Nothing was logged. The disks check what they store, the network checks what it carries, and the memory fixes flipped bits by itself. How sure can you be that all 1,000 files were unpacked correctly?
options: Certain: the disk and network checks would have caught any damage
Fairly sure: exit code 0 means every step worked
Not sure until something counts or recomputes the output: a processor or a bug can work out a wrong answer that no check below the program notices
Certain, because the memory corrects flipped bits
warmup.why: The disk and network checks protect bytes that are stored or sent, and the memory's checks repair bits that flip. None of them can tell that a processor worked out the wrong number. Meta found exactly this: one core of one processor returned 0 for one calculation, so some files were skipped as empty and the job finished normally. An exit code says that the code ran, not that its answers were right.

sections.h: A job that reports success and still loses files
sections.html:
Let's start with a real bug that Meta, the company behind Facebook, published in 2021. A job in Spark, a program that spreads big jobs over many computers, unpacked compressed files. To work out each file's size, it used a formula that called math.pow, a function that raises a number to a power. A processor, or CPU, is the chip that does a computer's arithmetic, and a core is one of the several calculators inside it. On one core of one CPU, core 59, Int(1.1^53) came out as 0 instead of 156, every time. 1.1^52 came out right.

Files whose size came out as 0 were skipped as empty. The job finished normally, and the database it fed was missing files. Nothing crashed and nothing was logged. No test had caught it.

This is silent data corruption: hardware that works out or stores a wrong value and raises no error. The Foundations track's lesson Faults, failures and the people who run systems gave the rate. Meta, Google and Alibaba, which each run hundreds of thousands of computers, report about 1 CPU in 1,000 that now and then computes wrong results without a word. Meta's paper, by Dixit and colleagues, tested hundreds of thousands of machines for silent errors and found hundreds of such CPUs.

Surely the checks built into every layer catch it? They don't, because each one guards something narrower. ECC memory, the kind most servers use, repairs a flipped bit in the computer's working memory. TCP sends data across a network in packets. It adds a checksum to each, a small number worked out from its bytes, so the receiver can spot a packet damaged on the way. TLS, the encryption on web connections, protects bytes on one connection. Each log record carries a check number of its own, a CRC-32C (Bytes, pages and durability, in the Storage engines track). It catches a record that was cut short or damaged on disk. All of them check that bytes arrived or stayed as they were. None can tell that the bytes were worked out wrongly in the first place, or that the code was wrong.

And code is wrong often enough. Databases have bugs that break their own promises. MySQL, another popular database program, had bug #73170 (2014), which left duplicates in an index, a sorted lookup list, that was meant to be unique. The authors of the Feral Concurrency Control study found a PostgreSQL bug in 2015 that let duplicates through at its strictest setting. Your own code has more: a message handed over twice and added twice, or a catch block, the code that handles an error, that quietly drops the one record that mattered.

The end-to-end argument, from the lesson of that name, applies here too. A check in a lower layer only makes problems rarer. The only complete check is at the ends, by code that knows what the data should be. Big storage systems already work this way. HDFS, a file system that spreads files over many machines, and S3, Amazon's storage service, run background scrubbers that read stored data back and compare the copies. The only way to know data is still there is to read it, and until you've restored a backup, you don't know that it works.

No layer below the app can tell a wrong answer from a right one. Check at the ends.

So the app has to check its own answers. Next, we'll set things up so that it can.

try.title: A core that gets one number wrong
steps: From the labs folder, run the demo below. It is Meta's bug made small: 1,000 files unpacked on 64 cores, where core 59 returns 0 for pow(1.1, 53) and the right answer for everything else.
Before it prints, predict what the job reports, and what the check at the end reports.
Read the excerpt. Which line would someone reviewing the code flag? (Probably none: the bug is in the hardware.)

code.title: MercurialCoreDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: private fun pow(core: Int, x: Double, y: Double): Double = if (core == 59 && x == 1.1 && y == 53.0) 0.0 else x.pow(y) // a mercurial core: wrong, and silent val size = pow(core, 1.1, level.toDouble()).toInt() * 4_096 if (size == 0) continue // "nothing to unpack"

try.expect:
job: unpacked 999 files, exit code 0, no errors logged
audit: 1000 files in, 999 files out, 1 missing
  file 59: level 53, unpacked on core 59
pow(1.1, 53) on a good core = 156, on core 59 = 0

The job reports success, because from its own point of view it succeeded: every step ran and nothing threw an error. Only the count at the end, files in against files out, notices the gap, and the details point straight at one core and one input. The demo's numbers are made up for teaching; the mechanism is the one in Meta's paper.

refs.title: Dixit et al., Silent Data Corruptions at Scale (2021)
MySQL bug #73170: duplicates in a unique secondary index

sections.h: Rebuild the view from its log, and compare it key by key
sections.html:
You can only check what you can work out again. Picture a table of balances changed in place by code that reads requests and calls other programs. There's no second opinion: the only record of what the table should hold is the table itself.

The design this track keeps coming back to fixes that. The log is the system of record, the official list of facts, and nothing ever changes it. Every view, a copy reshaped for one kind of question, is worked out from the log the same way every time: the same log in, the same view out. That's what derived data meant in the course's first lesson, What a data system is: something you can always rebuild from the record. So an audit job can replay the log from its first record, at offset (position) 0, into a fresh view. Then it compares that view key by key with the live one, and every difference is a bug.

Being able to rerun has a price. The code that builds a view can't read the clock, draw random numbers, or ask another program whose answer changes from one call to the next. If a fee depends on today's exchange rate, put the rate into the event when it happens, with the version of the fee rules and the time. Then the audit gets the same inputs the live code had.

The lab tries this on a ledger log of 5,000 postings. A ledger is a list of money movements, and each entry, one amount added to or taken from one account, is a posting. A live consumer, the program that reads the log and keeps a balance per account, runs once with no fault and once with each of five silent bugs. The rebuilt view finds all five, and each leaves its own fingerprint:

Bug in the live consumer Accounts off Total drift (cents) Grand totals match?
loses every 1,000th record 5 -12,056 no
is handed records 10 to 12 again after a crash 3 +8,420 no
one bit flipped in one stored balance 1 +1,048,576 (2^20) no
two flips that cancel 2 0 yes
cents cut off from record 2,500 on 497 -44,780 no

Lost records leave accounts short by exactly the lost amounts. Records handed over twice leave them over by exactly those amounts. A flipped bit leaves one account off by a power of two, here 2^20 cents, a sign of hardware rather than logic. Cutting off cents touches nearly every account, each by less than one unit per posting.

Look at the last column. Comparing grand totals, the sum of all balances against the sum of all postings, is called a reconciliation. It's cheap, and it caught four of the five. But two errors that cancel slip through: one account 16 cents up and another 16 cents down leave the total unchanged.

A total is an alarm. Only the key-by-key rebuild is an audit.

Sums and counts make good alarms that can run every minute. Run the full rebuild often enough to find a bug while the log still holds what you need to repair it. The same replay also repairs: fix the consumer, rebuild the view as a new version next to the old one, as Data integration did, and switch.

Here both views sat in one program's memory. Next, we'll compare two views far too big to send across a network.

try.title: Find five silent bugs by rebuilding
steps: From the labs folder, run the demo below. It runs the live consumer six times, once with no fault and once with each bug switched on, and audits each run.
Predict before it prints: which bug will the grand-total check miss? Which one changes the most accounts?
Look at the last column, merkle comparisons. Which bug makes that number big, and why? The next section explains.

code.title: AuditDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: val live = liveBalances(log, *faults) val drift = diff(live, truth) // key by key: the audit val totalsMatch = live.values.sum() == truth.values.sum() // one number: the alarm val m = compare(MerkleTree(truth), MerkleTree(live)) // 1,024 key ranges

try.expect:
fault                                   accounts off   total drift   totals match   merkle comparisons
no fault                                            0             0            yes                    1
drop every 1,000th record                           5        -12056             NO                   85
redeliver offsets 10..12 after a crash              3          8420             NO                   53
flip bit 20 of acct-123                             1       1048576             NO                   21
two flips that cancel in the total                  2             0            yes                   39
truncate cents from offset 2,500                  497        -44780             NO                 1599

The total check misses the two flips that cancel: one account went up by 16 cents and another down by 16. Cutting off cents changes 497 of 500 accounts. That is also the run where the Merkle comparison of the next section costs more (1,599 comparisons) than looking at all 1,024 ranges, because almost every range differs.

sections.h: A tree of hashes finds the drift without comparing every row
sections.html:
Rebuilding is the easy half of an audit. Say the live view has 50 million rows in the database that serves the app, and the rebuilt one sits in the warehouse, a separate database kept for analysis. Comparing them row by row means sending 50 million rows across the network every time you check.

What we need is a fingerprint for data. A hash function such as SHA-256 turns any amount of data into a short number of fixed size, 32 bytes, called its hash. The same data always gives the same hash, and any change, even of one bit, gives a different one. So two machines can compare a pile of rows by sending each other one hash each.

One hash for the whole view would say that something differs, but not where. A Merkle tree says where. Cut the keys into 2^k ranges (2 multiplied by itself k times: 1,024 for k = 10), using a hash of each key so the ranges come out even. The tree's bottom row has one leaf per range, the hash of every entry in that range, in key order. Above it, each parent is the hash of its two children, and so on up to a single root. The Replication track's lesson Leaderless replication met this tool keeping copies in step. Equal roots mean equal views, and different roots mean something differs.

Compare the roots first. If they differ, compare the two children, and go down only into a child that differs. One bad key in 1,024 ranges costs 1 + 2 x 10 = 21 comparisons: the root, then two children at each of ten levels. That's instead of 1,024 range comparisons, or 50 million row comparisons. Then you compare rows only inside the one range that was found. Each side builds its tree where its data lives, and only hashes cross the network until that last step.

The cost grows with the number of bad ranges, not the size of the view. The lab's numbers, for accounts with one flipped bit each:

Bad accounts 256 ranges 1,024 ranges 4,096 ranges
1 17 21 25
3 43 53 65
10 101 147 185
100 369 717 1,137

With 100 bad accounts in 256 ranges, the tree made more comparisons (369) than there are ranges. When most ranges differ, a plain scan is cheaper, and you have one big bug, not a hundred small ones, so a few ranges are enough to find it.

Merkle trees turn up wherever two copies of something big must be compared cheaply. Cassandra, a database that keeps several copies of each row, uses them to repair its copies. Git, which keeps a project's code history, uses them too, and so do the transparency logs of the next section. Next, we'll use hashes to check the log itself.

aside.title: Can two different piles of data have the same hash by chance?
aside.html: In principle, yes: there are endless possible inputs and only a fixed number of 32-byte hashes. In practice SHA-256 has 2^256 possible values, a number with 78 digits, so the chance that two different ranges match by accident is far too small to worry about. No one has published two different inputs with the same SHA-256 hash, even searching on purpose. That's why equal roots can be read as equal views.

sections.h: A chain of hashes shows the log wasn't rewritten, if someone else holds its head
sections.html:
The audit trusts the log. So what if the log itself changes? A disk might damage an old part of it, or someone with access might edit a posting from last month.

An old shop's receipt book had an answer: numbered pages with carbon copies, so a torn-out page leaves a gap. A hash chain does the same for a log. Each entry stores the hash of the entry before it, and its own hash covers that link and its contents. In code, hash = SHA-256(prev + payload), where prev is the previous entry's hash and payload is this entry's data. Edit entry 412, and its stored hash no longer matches what's in it. A verifier, a program that works the whole chain out again from the start, stops at exactly 412. That catches careless edits and damage on disk.

It doesn't catch an insider who controls the whole log. They can edit entry 412 and work out every later hash again, and the chain agrees with itself once more. The defence is to publish the head, the newest entry's hash, somewhere the log's owner can't change it. Send it every night to the auditors, the outside people who check the company's books. Or write it into another company's log, or print it in the payout report the bank signs. That's the receipt book's carbon copy, sent to head office. A verifier holding yesterday's head notices a rewritten history, and also a log whose newest entries were cut off. The lab builds all three attacks.

Transparency logs scale the idea up to logs the whole internet can check. Such a log keeps a Merkle tree over its entries and signs the root, with a digital signature only the log's owner can make. Anyone can ask for an inclusion proof, which shows that one entry is in the tree. It takes about log2(n) hashes, the number of times n can be halved: 20 for a million entries. Or they can ask for a consistency proof, which shows that today's tree still holds yesterday's, unchanged.

Certificate Transparency logs every certificate that browsers trust. A certificate is the signed ID card a website shows your browser to prove who it is (the Computer networking track's lesson TLS 1.3, certificates and mTLS). Chrome and Safari require certificates to carry signed timestamps from such logs, and monitors scan the logs for certificates issued for their own sites that they didn't ask for. No blockchain, a log shared by many parties who don't trust each other, is needed: each log has one writer, and others keep it honest by checking. Rekor, from Sigstore, a free project for signing software, does the same for the signatures on programs.

Ledger databases, databases sold with a hash chain built in, can disappear. AWS, Amazon's cloud business, shut its own, QLDB, on 31 July 2025. So build audit trails on mechanisms you can take with you: hash chains, Merkle proofs and logs you can export.

And remember what any of them proves. A chained or signed log shows that its entries weren't changed after they were written. It can't show that the right entries were written in the first place. That's the rebuild's job, and the job of the checks in the next section.

try.title: Three attacks on a hash-chained log
steps: From the labs folder, run the demo below. It builds a chain of 1,000 postings, keeps its head as "published", then attacks three fresh copies.
Predict each pair of answers. verify() checks the chain against itself, and verify(published) also compares the head. null means it found nothing wrong.
Which attack would a disk failure look like, and which ones need a person?

code.title: Model.kt (excerpt)
code.html: for (e in entries) { if (!e.prev.contentEquals(expectedPrev)) return e.index // a broken link if (!e.hash.contentEquals(sha256(e.prev, e.payload.toByteArray()))) return e.index // edited payload expectedPrev = e.hash } if (publishedHead != null && !head.contentEquals(publishedHead)) return size // rewritten or cut short

try.expect:
published head: f51e37f4efa835a8...
edit entry 412 in place:          verify() = 412, verify(published) = 412
edit 412 and recompute the rest:  verify() = null, verify(published) = 1000
drop the last 100 entries:        verify() = null, verify(published) = 900

An edit in place, which is what damage on disk looks like, fails the self-check at exactly entry 412. The other two attacks need someone who controls the log: working out every later hash again, or cutting off the newest entries. The chain alone can't see either. Only the head published before the attack can, and it reports where the published history and this one part ways.

sections.h: Check data where it arrives: quality checks and contracts
sections.html:
Many integrity bugs arrive from another team's code. Say the team that sends you payments starts sending amounts in whole euros instead of cents, renames a field, or sends empty values for a week. Every program that reads it works out wrong data, without a single error. A schema, the description of each field's name and type (the Encoding, APIs and workflows track's lesson Schemas that evolve), checks the shape of a record. An amount in cents and an amount in euros, both whole numbers, have exactly the same shape.

A data quality check is a rule about data, run like a test. A few kinds catch most problems:

  • Validity checks look at single values: not empty, unique, one of the allowed values, in a sane range (a card payment between 0.01 and 50,000.00).
  • Referential checks make sure that each payment's shop exists.
  • Freshness checks ask whether the newest record is less than an hour old.
  • Volume checks compare today's number of rows with the same day last week.
  • Reconciliation checks that two totals that should agree do agree.

In our payments app, the place to check hardest is the nightly payout. Each night the company pays every shop what it took that day, minus refunds and fees. People in payments call this settlement, and the list of payouts sent to the bank in the morning is the settlement file. In the lab it's a table, settlement_lines, with one row per payout. Once the bank has paid, the money can't be called back.

dbt, a free tool that builds tables from SQL queries (questions in the language most databases speak), has the first kinds built in as data tests: unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships. They run after a table is built and return the rows that break them. Its model contracts check one step earlier: with contract: enforced: true, the build fails if a table's columns and types don't match what was declared.

A data contract writes down what the team that produces the data promises, and what the teams that use it rely on, so that a machine can check it. It holds the schema, what each field means and in which units, the allowed values, freshness and volume targets, and who owns it. The Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS), from the Bitol project at the Linux Foundation, is a format for these in YAML, a plain-text format for settings. Its site lists version 3.2.0. A contract helps only if something runs it: the producing team's automatic tests before a change ships, and the using team's checks before data is used.

Where checks run matters as much as what they check. At the producer, before publishing, a failure is cheapest to fix. At the consumer, before building views, a check protects you from someone else's bug. On outputs, before anything you can't undo, a check is the last line: compare the settlement file with the ledger before it goes to the bank.

When a check fails, stop the line. Hold the batch back, alert a person, and keep the bad data out of the views. A check that only logs a warning is the catch block that dropped the record, all over again.

Every check in this lesson compares data with the log or with rules someone wrote down. None of them asks whether the data should exist at all. The next lesson does.

try.title: Write the checks for the settlement table
steps: The table settlement_lines has one row per payout: payout_id, merchant_id (the shop), amount_cents, currency and settled_on (the day). It is built every night from the ledger and sent to the bank in the morning.
Write down five checks, at least one of each kind: validity, referential, freshness or volume, and reconciliation. For each, say which bug it would catch.
Decide which ones must pass before the file goes to the bank, and what the job should do when one fails.
try.expect:
One reasonable set, in dbt's YAML plus one SQL check (yours will differ):

models:
  - name: settlement_lines
    columns:
      - name: payout_id
        data_tests: [unique, not_null]          # a payout sent twice, or with no id
      - name: merchant_id
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              arguments: {to: ref('merchants'), field: merchant_id}   # a payout to nobody
      - name: currency
        data_tests:
          - accepted_values:
              arguments: {values: ['EUR', 'GBP', 'USD']}

-- reconciliation: returns a row (a failure) if the file and the ledger disagree
SELECT s.total, l.total
FROM (SELECT sum(amount_cents) AS total FROM settlement_lines WHERE settled_on = :day) s,
     (SELECT sum(cents) AS total FROM ledger_postings WHERE kind = 'payout' AND day = :day) l
WHERE s.total <> l.total;

Add a volume check (a row count within 30% of the same weekday last week) to catch a half-built file, and a range check on amount_cents to catch the switch from cents to whole euros. The uniqueness, reconciliation and volume checks must pass before sending, because the bank can't un-send money. When one fails, the job keeps the file back, alerts the person on duty and leaves yesterday's state in place. It never sends a file "with warnings".

opening:
Picture a café owner checking her bank account on Monday morning. The payments company pays her every night for the day's card sales, and the weekend's money is there. It looks about right, so she doesn't think twice. It's 12.40 short. One payment in two hundred never made it into the total, and every program reported success.

It's easy to believe that a wrong number would make a noise somewhere. Disks check what they store, networks check what they carry, and a program that fails usually says so. Those checks are real, which is exactly why we trust them.

In Constraints without coordination, we promised integrity everywhere: nothing lost, nothing made up. That promise assumed the machines did what the code said. In this lesson, we'll drop that assumption. We'll watch a processor get one sum wrong in silence, rebuild a view to catch hidden bugs, find the bad part of a huge view with a tree of hashes, and prove that a log wasn't rewritten. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café owner paid 12.40 too little while every program reported success. Nothing on the way could tell a wrong sum from a right one. Only a check at the end could: rebuild the view from the log, and compare it key by key.

Next time your bank sends a statement, add up a few days of payments yourself and compare them with how the balance moved. That's a small reconciliation, the cheap alarm. If the two disagree, the list of payments is the record to trust.

Next, we'll turn from the machines to the people the records describe, and ask what a data system owes them.

compare.title: A reconciliation and an audit

a.label: Reconciliation
a.title: one number per side
a.html: -- cheap, runs every minute; misses errors that cancel SELECT (SELECT sum(cents) FROM ledger_postings WHERE day = :day) AS from_log, (SELECT sum(delta) FROM balance_changes WHERE day = :day) AS from_view;

b.label: Recompute and diff
b.title: every key
b.html: // replay the log into a fresh view, then compare key by key val expected = sortedMapOf<String, Long>() for (p in log) expected[p.account] = (expected[p.account] ?: 0L) + p.cents val drift = (live.keys + expected.keys).toSortedSet() .filter { live[it] != expected[it] } .map { Drift(it, live[it], expected[it]) }

compare.note: The reconciliation compares two numbers and costs almost nothing, so it can run all the time as an alarm. It can't say which account is wrong, and two errors of opposite sign cancel in it. The rebuild costs a replay of the log and one comparison per key. It finds every difference and its size, which is what you need to repair the view. Use the first as the smoke alarm and the second as the inspection, with a Merkle tree in between when the two views live far apart.

worked.title: Check a three-entry hash chain by hand

steps.say: Entry 0 links to a starting hash of 32 zero bytes, since nothing comes before it. Its hash covers that link and its payload. (These are real SHA-256 values, cut to 12 hexadecimal digits.)
Each later entry stores the hash before it as its prev. The last hash is the head, and it goes to the auditors.
steps.code:
hash1 = sha256(hash0 + "1,acct-123,-400") = 868b50f834cd...
hash2 = sha256(hash1 + "2,acct-007,9999") = 1fe40a4c193a...
published head = 1fe40a4c193a...

steps.say: Someone edits entry 1 from -400 to -40 and leaves the hashes alone. The verifier works out entry 1's hash again and compares it with the stored one.
steps.code:
sha256(hash0 + "1,acct-123,-40") = e9b57bd3945e...
stored hash1                      = 868b50f834cd...   -> mismatch: verify() = 1

steps.say: An insider does better: edits entry 1 and works out hash1 and hash2 again, so every link checks out.
steps.code:
hash1' = e9b57bd3945e...   entry 2's prev = hash1'
hash2' = 37f55def423f...   verify() = null (consistent with itself)

steps.say: The published head catches it. The chain's head is now hash2', and the auditors hold the old one.

lab.title: Audit a view: rebuild it, compare it with a Merkle tree, chain its log
steps: From the labs folder, run the tests once. 19 tests run, and all fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's way of saying "not written yet". Ledger.kt is finished: the ledger log made from a fixed seed, the live consumer, and its four faults you can switch on.
In Audit.kt, write recompute and diff. Run AuditTest. Each fault test checks the fingerprint its bug should leave, such as accounts short by exactly the lost amounts.
In Merkle.kt, write buildInternalNodes and compare. Run MerkleTest. The 21-comparison test fails if your walk looks at the children of nodes that already match.
In HashChain.kt, write append and verify. Run HashChainTest, and note which two attacks only the published head catches.
If you have time, add a fault of your own to Ledger.kt, such as postings for acct-007 applied to acct-070, and predict its fingerprint before you compare.
hints: recompute: for (p in log) view[p.account] = (view[p.account] ?: 0L) + p.cents, with view a sortedMapOf.
diff: take (live.keys + expected.keys).toSortedSet(), keep the keys where live[it] != expected[it], and turn each one into a Drift.

compare: a local recursive fun visit(node: Int) that counts, returns on equal hashes, records node - leaves for a leaf, and otherwise visits 2 * node then 2 * node + 1. Compare byte arrays with contentEquals, never ==, which only asks whether they are the same object.
verify: keep expectedPrev, starting at GENESIS. Check the link, then the hash, then move expectedPrev on. Compare the head with publishedHead only after the loop.

drill.title: Audits from memory
drill.prompt: Without notes: (1) write compare for two Merkle trees stored as arrays (root at 1, the children of node i at 2i and 2i + 1, leaves from leaves on); (2) give the number of comparisons for one bad key among 2^k ranges; (3) name what a hash chain catches on its own, and the two attacks that need a published head; (4) say why comparing grand totals is not an audit.

answer.html: // (1) fun compare(a: MerkleTree, b: MerkleTree): MerkleDiff { val found = ArrayList<Int>() var n = 0 fun visit(node: Int) { n++ if (a.nodes[node].contentEquals(b.nodes[node])) return if (node >= a.leaves) { found += node - a.leaves; return } visit(2 * node); visit(2 * node + 1) } visit(1) return MerkleDiff(found, n) } // (2) 1 + 2k: the root, then two children at each of k levels (21 for 1,024 ranges) // (3) alone: any entry edited in place (corruption, careless edits), at its index; // with a published head: a rewrite that recomputes every later hash, and truncation // (4) errors of opposite sign cancel in a sum, and a total can't say which key is wrong

recap: Hardware, databases and your own code produce wrong data without raising errors: about 1 CPU in 1,000 at the biggest companies, and Meta's core 59 returned 0 for 1.1^53. The checks in memory, disks and networks protect bytes in one place, not the arithmetic.

Design so you can check: a log that never changes, and views worked out only from it, let a job rebuild any view and compare it key by key. Each bug leaves a fingerprint. Comparing totals is an alarm, not an audit.
A Merkle tree compares two big views by swapping hashes: 1 + 2 log2(n) comparisons for one bad range among n, then a row-by-row check of that range only.

A hash chain shows an entry edited in place on its own; a head published where the owner can't change it also shows a rewritten history or a cut-off end. Transparency logs (Certificate Transparency, Rekor) scale this up with Merkle proofs, and QLDB's shutdown argues for mechanisms you can take with you.

Check data where it crosses from one team to another: validity, referential, freshness, volume and reconciliation checks, and data contracts that both sides run. A failed check stops the line before anything you can't undo.
The limit: every check here compares data with the log or with written rules. A chained log can't show that the right entries went in, and no check says whether the data should exist at all.

explain.prompt: A friend's team builds a payments app. They ask why they should spend time on an audit job when "the database keeps our transactions safe, the disks keep copies, and Kafka, the program that keeps our log, checks every record." Explain what those things promise, what they don't, and what the audit adds.
explain.answer: Each of those protects bytes against one kind of fault in one place. The database makes each transaction happen all or nothing, the copies survive a dead disk, and Kafka's check numbers catch a damaged record. None of them checks that the numbers we wrote were the right numbers. A consumer that applies a posting twice writes a perfectly valid, perfectly copied, correctly checked wrong balance. A processor can work out a wrong value without any error, which Meta and Google see in about 1 CPU in 1,000. And databases have bugs too, such as a MySQL bug that left duplicates in an index meant to be unique. The audit job is the check at the end: it replays the log, which never changes, into a fresh view and compares it with the live one, account by account, so any drift is found while the log still holds what we need to fix it. A Merkle tree makes that comparison cheap when the two views live on different machines. And a hash chain, with a head we send to the auditors, shows that the log itself wasn't changed.

deeper.html:
Ledger products come and go. Amazon QLDB packaged a hash-chained journal as a managed database. When AWS shut it down on 31 July 2025, it pointed customers to Aurora PostgreSQL, Amazon's own version of PostgreSQL, which keeps no history that can't be changed, so audit history has to be built and kept outside it. immudb (v1.11.2 in September 2026) is an open-source ledger database, with its code public.

Mercurial cores at Google. In the same year as Meta's paper, Google's "Cores that don't count" (Hochschild and colleagues, HotOS 2021) described CPU cores that now and then compute wrong results, which they called mercurial, and reported seeing a few per several thousand machines. Both companies now run tests for silent errors across all their machines and take suspect cores out of service. You can't run their tests, but you can use their idea: for important calculations, compute twice on different machines and compare.

How transparency logs stay cheap. Certificate Transparency is defined in RFC 6962 (2013) and, as version 2.0, in RFC 9162 (2021); RFCs are the documents that define internet standards. A log promises to add each certificate within its maximum merge delay, usually 24 hours, and returns a signed timestamp at once. Monitors download new entries and check them. Anyone who has seen two signed tree heads can ask for a consistency proof that the later tree extends the earlier one. A log that shows different trees to different people is caught as soon as two of them compare heads, which is why monitors share the heads they see. Newer logs serve the tree as static tiles, files that any web cache can serve. That's the design behind Rekor v2, released as rekor-tiles (v2.4.1 in October 2026).

Reads are events too. If a fraud decision depends on what a model saw, log what it saw: its inputs, the model version and the score, with the decision's request ID. Then an audit can rebuild the decision as well as the balance, and the next lesson shows why that record matters to people who want to challenge a decision.

The case for auditing derived data end to end is made in Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 13.
